title: Seminar on Religions and beliefs in the city: “Possibilities, practices, and problems”
content: The diversity of religions and beliefs shapes urban space and impacts the everyday life of cities in schools, workplaces, public spaces, and public discourse. How can we act equitably in the continuously evolving religious reality? How can we respond to challenges related to diversity of beliefs? How can we leverage the opportunities related to religions and beliefs?

title: Visit from the University of Washington
content:
Last Thursday we had visitors from the University of Washington in Seattle, when Prof. Scott B. Radnitz, Prof. Andrew Nestingen, and 17 bachelor's students joined our master's thesis seminar. The group is currently on a three-week excursion through Finland and Estonia, exploring the Nordic-Baltic region and topics such as security questions of our region.

Andrew Nestingen is a professor and former chair of Scandinavian Studies at UW and an expert in Nordic culture and media, while Scott Radnitz is the Herbert J. Ellison Professor of Russian and Eurasian Studies at UW's Henry M. Jackson School of International Studies, with expertise in post-Soviet countries and security dynamics, among other topics.

The visit is also a great step toward building stronger ties between the University of Washington and the University of Helsinki.

After the seminar, we wrapped up the day with drinks at Thirsty Scholar. Thank you for stopping by, and we hope you had a great time and an amazing trip!”

title: Miten autoritaarinen Venäjä on selviytynyt talousvaikeuksistaan sodan aikana?
content:
Since the start of the Russian military assault on Ukraine in 2022, numerous experts and observers have predicted that the Russian economy would fail due to the excessive costs of the war.

Economic responses to Russian aggression, ranging from severe sanctions imposed by Western powers to recent Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries and logistical networks, have aimed at substantially increasing these costs.

However, despite mounting costs, the Russian wartime economy has demonstrated remarkable resilience – at least in the short term. There are no signs that it would collapse any time soon. How can we explain this resilience, and what might we expect for the future?

After the turbulent period of market reforms, the deep and protracted recession of the 1990s, and the spectacular rebound of the 2000s, Russia built and consolidated a politico-economic model during the 2010s that can be labeled as a predatory state.

It is based upon direct and indirect state control over key strategic sectors of the economy, such as energy and the military-industrial complex, often managed by personal friends and cronies of the top political leadership.

title: “Ilman pölyttäjiä maailma olisi ankea ja väritön” – Uusi näyttely avaa oven pölyttäjien kiehtovaan elämään
content:
Pollinators represent an astonishingly diverse group of animals, many of which possess remarkable abilities despite their small size. Bees can count, bumblebees solve problems, and on distant islands, even lizards can pollinate flowers.

The  exhibition, which combines science and art, offers a wealth of information, stunning visuals, and fun activities for visitors of all ages. Guests can play interactive games like "Identify the Pollinators" and "Pollinator Protection Bingo," design their own imaginary pollinator, and explore the museum's impressive collection of specimens. The exhibition is based on a newly illustrated non-fiction book.

– We want to show the world through the eyes of pollinators, says exhibition scriptwriter Mia Rönkä, Adjunct Professor in Environmental Ecology at the University of Turku. Rönkä has written the exhibition’s informational texts and poems.

Although the sensory perceptions, cognitive abilities, and communication methods of pollinators like bees differ from ours as humans, we can still strive to understand and appreciate them as individuals of other species – without anthropomorphizing them, Rönkä explains.

title: Arkadiankadun siltaremontti aiheuttaa muutoksia liikennejärjestelyihin Luonnontieteellisen museon lähistöllä
content:
The renovation will start with the construction of temporary traffic arrangements from Wednesday 7 January onwards. The renovation is expected to be completed in late 2026.

A temporary bridge for pedestrians will be built on the east side of Arkadiankatu over the Baana. The aim is to maintain the pedestrian route on the east side of the bridge until the temporary bridge is operational. Cyclists will also be able to use the bridge.

The Baana route underneath the bridge is expected to remain open for most of the renovation's duration, with some minor exceptions.

There will be changes to the motor vehicle routes by the bridge and around it in January. If possible, should be favoured during the bridge renovation.

Connections to the bus terminals in Kamppi will remain available, but there will be a slight diversion of routes.

Trams 1 and 1T will run via Simonkatu and Kamppi. Lasipalatsi and the Natural History Museum will not be served.

The diversion is due to the renovation of the Arkadiankatu bridge and will remain in place until late 2026. The renovation will not affect HSL's bus services.

title: Ukrainan sota - yliopiston suositukset
content:
The University of Helsinki has condemned the military action by Russia and expressed its support for Ukraine and its university community. We have also expressed our support for Ukraine, together with other Finnish universities, through statements by and the . As a demonstration of support, we have illuminated buildings in the colours of the Ukrainian flag and raised the flag on our premises.

One of the principles of the University of Helsinki is to promote international collaboration in research and higher education, and to support these efforts even in difficult circumstances. Russia’s indefensible military aggression in Ukraine has required exceptional measures, which include those taken in the collaboration between universities.

The University of Helsinki is monitoring both national and EU-level sanctions, adapting our policies and processes accordingly. Together with other Finnish and international universities, the University of Helsinki strives to promote the end of military action in Ukraine, while supporting Ukrainian institutions and people.

title: Vaikea RSV-infektio voi lisätä lapsen riskiä sairastua astmaan varhaislapsuudessa
content:
Originally published on the HUS website on 9 September, 2026.

Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is one of the most common causes of respiratory infection in young children. Severe RSV infection in infancy has been associated with wheezing and asthma later in childhood. However, it has remained unclear whether RSV itself causes asthma, or whether the same children are inherently susceptible to both severe RSV infection and asthma.

A study by HUS, the University of Helsinki's Institute for Molecular Medicine Finland (FIMM), Finnish Institute for Health and Welfare, and Nordic collaborative partners investigated this question by combining national Finnish registry data with genetic analyses. The study included nearly a million children born in Finland between 1998 and 2014. The genetic component was based on genomic data from nearly 100,000 participants in Nordic genetic cohorts.


The study investigated how many children with recurrent wheezing or asthma had been hospitalized with RSV during the first year of their life, and how their clinical characteristics differed from other children with asthma.

title: Kielipankissa: Sanna Nordlund
content:
I am Sanna Nordlund, a doctoral researcher at the  at the University of Jyväskylä. My research focuses on the structure of Finnish Sign Language from a corpus-based perspective. I am currently funded by a grant from the Finnish Cultural Foundation and have previously received a multi-year grant from the Kone Foundation. My previous experience includes serving as a substitute lecturer in the Sign Language Interpreter programme at Humak University of Applied Sciences (2023–2024) and working on the  at the Finnish Association of the Deaf (2013–2015). Prior to pursuing an academic career, I also worked as a sign language interpreter.

As a sign language researcher, I draw on and combine the knowledge and skills I acquired through my studies in general linguistics with the expertise I gained through my education and professional experience as a sign language interpreter. I also serve as one of the group leaders of the  within the Langnet doctoral network.
